description:
We are a two-member team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, excited to explore new ideas, learn new technologies, and create something meaningful together.

As SenseSphere, we are passionate about innovation, technology, and solving real-world challenges. We are currently exploring ways to make NASA Earth science information more accessible through creative and interactive experiences.

We believe in curiosity, collaboration, experimentation, and learning along the way.
summary: SenseSphere is an interactive “Earth Jukebox” that turns NASA Earth observation visualizations into live sound, so people can hear the planet as well as see it. It sonifies two NASA Scientific Visualization Studio datasets: night lights 2012–2023, including a change map, and lightning flashes detected from the ISS 2017–2023. HTML5 Canvas analyzes video frames in real time and Tone.js generates the audio, mapping position and brightness to pitch, volume and stereo panning on a musical scale. A sweeping line plays the night lights it passes, with new lights and lights-out areas sounding different, while the lightning globe plays newly detected flashes. A soft generated chord pad adds atmosphere under the data notes. SenseSphere is designed to support blind and low-vision users with keyboard controls, a mute button and screen-reader announcements, though it has not yet been tested with them.
details:
What it does and how it works: SenseSphere is a browser-based "Earth Jukebox" that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live sound. An off-screen HTML5 Canvas analyzes video frames pixel by pixel, and Tone.js generates the audio in real time. For night lights, a vertical line sweeps across the map and plays the lights it passes. Higher on the map means a higher note and brighter means louder. In the change map, purple (new lights) plays a higher chime and orange (lights out) a lower tone. For lightning, the app detects newly appearing yellow flashes on a rotating globe. Horizontal position sets pitch and stereo panning, and flashes in the upper half play an octave higher. All notes are snapped to a pentatonic scale so the result stays musical.

Benefits: It gives people another way to explore satellite data, through hearing instead of sight alone. It works in any modern browser with no installation, and the controls work from the keyboard.

Intended impact: SenseSphere is designed to support blind and low-vision users, and to help teachers and science communicators make Earth data more engaging. It has not yet been tested with blind or low-vision users.

Tools, languages, hardware and software: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript; the Canvas API; Tone.js (Web Audio); FFmpeg for converting the NASA videos; NASA Scientific Visualization Studio visualizations. No special hardware is needed, only a laptop and a web browser.

How it is creative: It translates two very different visualizations into sound with different logic, a sweeping scan for the night lights and flash-by-flash notes for the lightning. A soft generated chord pad sits under the data notes for atmosphere, and the notes are kept distinct so the data stays audible.

Factors we considered: Musicality (notes snapped to a scale so raw data doesn't sound like noise), clarity (limiting how many notes play at once), and accessibility (keyboard controls, a mute button, an adjustable brightness threshold, a live text readout and screen-reader announcements). Limitations: the lightning map shows a 10-day window of ISS detections, so it reflects seasonal patterns and not live lightning, and covers only tropical and mid-latitude regions. The globe rotates, so left and right describe screen position. Year-to-year night-light changes are subtle, so the change map is where the difference is clearest.
